title: Autopsy report on son's death puzzles parents
article: The chief medical examiner's report on the death of a 19-year-old man while in police custody has his parents demanding an independent autopsy.
Wilfred Asham died early on the morning of Sept. 2 in a holding room at the downtown Public Safety Building.

He'd been taken into custody at around 1 a.m. for the alleged theft of a minivan. Less than 20 minutes after he arrived, Asham reportedly went into convulsions. Police called paramedics, who were unable to revive him.
Family members say the report on Asham's death, which they say they are legally unable to distribute, found no traces of hard drugs in his system.
The toxicology report did find trace amounts of marijuana, said Asham's stepfather, Louis Vosters, and a blood alcohol level of 0.118. The legal limit in Manitoba is 0.08.
The autopsy also found Asham had a "probable heart arrhythmia," said Vosters, something the family found to be puzzling.
"He had no heart problem," said Asham's mother, Sheila McKenzie.
McKenzie said the report could not conclude whether the heart condition was the reason for Asham's death.
"According to the coroner, they're saying that it cannot be proven, either that caused it or didn't cause it," said McKenzie.

The report's description of bruising on Asham's face and neck as "unremarkable" was particularly upsetting, said Vosters. The family has contended that Asham's nose was crooked before his death, but appeared to have been straightened when his body was seen at the funeral. They also said facial bruising was clearly visible after his death.
"They're saying no remarkable trauma to the head. At the funeral there was obvious signs of trauma to the head," said McKenzie.
The family isn't satisfied with the results of the report, and said they're working with a lawyer to seek an independent review.
Police could not be reached for comment. However, their investigation into Asham's death is still underway.
